etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English dignyte, from Old French dignité, from Latin dignitās (“worthiness, merit, dignity, grandeur, authority, rank, office”), from dignus (“worthy, appropriate”), from Proto-Italic *degnos, from Proto-Indo-European *dḱ-nos, from *deḱ- (“to take”). See also decus (“honor, esteem”) and decet (“it is fitting”). Cognate to deign. Doublet of dainty. In this sense, displaced native Old English weorþsċipe, which became Modern English worship.

definitions.definition: The state of being dignified or worthy of esteem: elevation of mind or character.

quote.citation: 1751 December (indicated as 1752), Henry Fielding, chapter VIII, in Amelia. […], volume I, London:  […]  [William Strahan] for A[ndrew] Millar […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He uttered this ... with great majesty, or, as he called it, dignity.

quote.citation: 1981, African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, art. 5:
quote.text: Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being.

quote.citation: 1905, E. M. Forster, Where Angels Fear to Tread , chapter 7, third paragraph:
quote.text: The reception room was sacred to the dead wife. Her shiny portrait hung upon the wall - similar, doubtless, in all respects to the one which would be pasted on her tombstone. A little piece of black drapery had been tacked above the frame to lend a dignity to woe. But two of the tacks had fallen out, and the effect was now rakish, as that of a drunkard's bonnet.

quote.citation: 1934, Aldous Huxley, “Puerto Barrios”, in Beyond the Mexique Bay:
quote.text: Official DIGNITY tends to increase in inverse ratio to the importance of the country in which the office is held.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act III, scene iii:
quote.text: Note the preſumption of this Scythian ſlaue:I tel thee villaine, thoſe that lead my horſeHaue to their names tytles of dignitie,And dar’ſt thou bluntly cal me Baiazeth?

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Esther 6:3:
quote.text: And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this?

quote.citation: 1781, Edward Gibbon, The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, F. III. 231:
quote.text: He ... distributed the civil and military dignities among his favourites and followers.

definitions.definition: One holding high rank; a dignitary.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jude 1:8:
quote.text: These filthy dreamers  […]  speak evil of dignities.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Sciences concluding from dignities, and principles known by themselves.
